transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-18 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (CTO - Helix), Priya Nair (Head of ML), Samir Gupta (Infra), Nora Bishop (PM)

Summary: quick intake focused on unit economics and hosting decision; customer provided QPS targets and compliance constraints; next steps include benchmark and pricing spreadsheet.

[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro, I'm Jordan, I'll run the commercial side.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Hi, Maya here, I'll handle the technical bits, happy to deep dive into latency and batching.
[00:22] Alex Rivera: Alex — we run the platform side at Helix, primarily interested in cost predictability and keeping sensitive models on premises or at least inside our VPC.
[00:32] Priya Nair: Priya — head of ML, curious about token costs and quality tradeoffs if we quantize.
[00:38] Samir Gupta: Samir — infra, I'll be the one worrying about network egress, KMS keys, and firewall rules.
[00:45] Nora Bishop: Nora — product, aligning timelines and success criteria.

[01:05] Jordan Patel: Great. To frame — we want to understand the workload: traffic shape, average and max QPS, prompt lengths, and what you consider acceptable tail latency. That lets us show you per-token pricing vs reserved seat math.
[01:24] Priya Nair: For our main recommender flow it's pretty chatty — average sequence about 120 tokens per inference, but we have a long tail where some sessions go up to 2k tokens. Baseline 400–800 QPS normally, spikes to ~2k for big batch windows.
[01:44] Maya Chen: ok, that tail matters. Two levers we usually suggest: batching for steady-state throughput and prefix/KV caching for repeated context — dramatic per-token savings if you can cache prefixes.
[02:03] Alex Rivera: Can you quantify that? If we put caching in front does that drop billable tokens or just server load?
[02:10] Maya Chen: it reduces billable tokens because if a prefix is cached we avoid re-generation for that portion; the runtime will still compute the new tokens but cached KV avoids the full decode cost in many cases. In practice for recommender sessions we've seen effective token savings of 15–40% depending on prompt reuse.
[02:34] Priya Nair: 15–40% is useful. Our challenge is unpredictability — the reuse pattern changes with product features.

[03:00] Samir Gupta: From an infra angle, we need to know network hops — hosted means traffic leaves our VPC to Redwood endpoints, dedicated POC could be colocated or RB, and private is fully in our VPC. KMS integration is a hard requirement for us.
[03:18] Jordan Patel: For Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations and audit logs; hosted can also be configured with customer key wraps in many cases — we'll put the specifics in the security pack.
[03:33] Alex Rivera: SLA expectations — we need P99 <= 200ms for our 95% of requests, and P99.9 ideally under 600ms. Is that realistic?
[03:48] Maya Chen: For short sequences (<=256 tokens) we can hit sub-100ms p99 on Dedicated shapes with batching tuned. Hosted will be close but depends on routing and regional capacity; fallback to a smaller, cheaper model increases reliability but can impact quality.
[04:10] Priya Nair: Quality tradeoff is important — we won't accept routing to a model that drops our key metrics by more than 5% without notice.
[04:18] Maya Chen: understood; rollouts can be configured with canary/AB and automatic fallback, and you can pin model versions. We'll recommend A/B thresholds for quality regressions.

[05:00] Jordan Patel: Let's talk dollars — you gave us a rough budget signal in the intake form, can you restate your target unit cost?
[05:10] Nora Bishop: We're targeting roughly $0.0009–$0.0015 per token for the high-volume recommender path — if we can get under a cent per token it's a win.
[05:24] Jordan Patel: That range is common. For hosted, per-token is usage-based; batching and caching reduce effective tokens. For Dedicated there's a committed monthly capacity which lowers unit cost as throughput increases.
[05:40] Maya Chen: Quantization also helps — 8-bit or 4-bit variants can cut GPU cost but sometimes need a small eval to ensure quality doesn't drop.
[05:52] Priya Nair: We're concerned about hallucinations if quantized.
[05:57] Maya Chen: totally — we run a prompt-level regression suite during quantization to validate.

[06:30] Alex Rivera: Can you give a concrete worked example — say 1M tokens/day, average 120 tokens per call, what's the hosted bill vs dedicated?
[06:42] Jordan Patel: Sure. Rough math: 1M tokens/day is ~30M tokens/month. On Hosted, at list price for this model family that's around $X/token — (note: Jordan clarifies numbers) — depending on model and caching you might be in the $0.0012 - $0.0018 range. With Dedicated and a reserved pool sized to your peak, amortized GPU cost brings it down to $0.0006–$0.0010 effective token, before additional infra and licensing.
[07:14] Priya Nair: So there's an inflection point where Dedicated is cheaper if volume is steady. What's that break-even?
[07:22] Maya Chen: ballpark: if you sustain >15–20M tokens/month with predictable traffic, Dedicated generally looks better. But caching and batching can shift that.

[08:00] Samir Gupta: What about burst handling — if we get a sudden spike to 2k QPS, does Dedicated have burst capacity?
[08:08] Jordan Patel: Yes, we offer burst pools on Dedicated and cross-region fallback. There's an extra charge for burst but it's cheaper than overprovisioning permanently.

[09:00] Priya Nair: On benchmarks, we want end-to-end p99 including network. Will Redwood run an end-to-end pilot from our infra to the model to measure that?
[09:12] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we can run a 72-hour benchmark simulating your QPS profile using your prompt set. We'll measure token throughput, p50/p95/p99, KV cache hit rates, and effective tokens billed. We'll also run quantized vs full-precision runs if you want.
[09:36] Alex Rivera: That sounds good. We need to capture auditability too — will you provide logs showing which keys were used and when?
[09:45] Jordan Patel: We provide detailed audit logs and token-level usage breakdowns in the Console; for Private we can route logs to your SIEM. We'll attach the security pack with exact retention and log format.

[10:30] Nora Bishop: Timeline — if we kick off the benchmark this week what does the onboarding look like?
[10:37] Maya Chen: Typical: 1) exchange keys/credentials and sample prompts, 2) Redwood sets up benchmark harness, 3) run 72 hours, 4) analysis call with results and a pricing model. We can do step 1 in 2–3 business days.

[11:12] Jordan Patel: On pricing documentation — I'll send a worksheet that models Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with your traffic inputs so you can play with caching rates and batching latencies.
[11:23] Priya Nair: Good — also include an example where we quantize and the quality regressions are tracked.

[12:00] Alex Rivera: A few gotchas — tokenization differences across model families, sometimes our instrumenting shows different token counts than vendors report. Any advice?
[12:10] Maya Chen: We recommend you share raw prompts and we'll token-count on our side; also we'll output both raw tokens and billed tokens in the benchmark so you can reconcile.

[12:40] Samir Gupta: Security specifics — our compliance team requires KMS wrapping with customer-managed key, SOC2 report, and an architecture diagram showing private endpoints.
[12:52] Jordan Patel: Noted. We have SOC2 Type II, we support CMK via major cloud KMS providers, and for Private we can do a VPC-only dataplane. We'll drop those artifacts in the security pack.

[13:30] Speaker 2: Is there support for on-premises air-gapped deployment?
[13:35] Maya Chen: Yes, we offer an on-prem package for highly regulated customers; that typically involves a different sales and implementation path and minimum commitment.

[14:00] Priya Nair: What's the expected uplift in operational complexity if we go Dedicated or Private vs Hosted?
[14:10] Maya Chen: Dedicated requires some capacity planning and occasional tuning; Private has the most operational work on the customer's side for networking and keys, but we provide deployment playbooks and managed support options.

[15:00] Jordan Patel: Let's talk fallback safety — you mentioned not accepting a >5% quality drop. We can set up monitoring that alerts on prompt-level regressions and automatically rollback traffic if thresholds breach.

[16:20] Alex Rivera: That monitoring ties into our SRE workflows — can alerts be routed into PagerDuty and our Slack?
[16:28] Maya Chen: Yes, we have integrations for Slack, PagerDuty, and can stream traces to your observability pipeline.

[17:05] Priya Nair: One more on economics — what about model choice? If we pick a slightly smaller model that's 30% cheaper but only 2% worse on our metrics, that might be preferable. Can Redwood run side-by-side evals?
[17:20] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we can run evals across model variants and show tradeoffs in quality vs cost. Those results feed into the pricing worksheet.

[18:00] Nora Bishop: Procurement question — do you accept net-30 and what kind of contract length for Dedicated?
[18:08] Jordan Patel: For Dedicated we usually do monthly or annual commitments; terms (net-30) are negotiable for enterprise deals. We'll loop legal in once you indicate direction.

[19:00] Alex Rivera: Anything we should be aware of for our security team before the demo?
[19:07] Jordan Patel: We'll send an initial security pack and an architecture diagram. If your team wants a live security deep dive we can schedule a separate call with our security lead.

[20:00] Priya Nair: ok, for the benchmark, we'll provide 200 representative prompts and the QPS time-series. Expecting to see cache hit rate, billed tokens, latency percentiles.

[21:15] Maya Chen: Great. On the caching front, if you can mark session-anchored prompts (where early tokens repeat) we can set caching TTLs to maximize savings.

[22:00] Samir Gupta: Are there SDKs for instrumentation? We want to collect per-request metadata for correlation.
[22:08] Maya Chen: Yes — we have SDKs and trace hooks for per-request ids; we can also accept OpenTelemetry spans.

[23:00] Jordan Patel: Let's recap and align on next steps.
[23:06] Jordan Patel: Action items: Jordan will send pricing worksheet and security pack; Maya will send benchmark plan; Priya and Samir will share prompts and infra constraints.
[23:22] Priya Nair: Sounds right. I can get the prompts together by Monday.
[23:28] Samir Gupta: I'll send network/VPC constraints and KMS requirements by Tuesday.

[24:00] Nora Bishop: Timeline to decision — if benchmark looks good we could be ready to sign a Dedicated pilot in January.
[24:10] Jordan Patel: Perfect. We'll aim to have the bench results and a proposed Dedicated shape by the end of the week after the benchmark.

[25:00] Alex Rivera: Quick nit — any hidden fees or egress costs?
[25:07] Jordan Patel: For Hosted, standard egress and additional snapshotting have nominal fees; Dedicated includes data plane costs in the committed price but cross-region egress is billed separately. We'll call that out in the worksheet.

[26:00] Priya Nair: Ok, that's all from us.
[26:05] Jordan Patel: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and scheduling.

[26:20] Maya Chen: Thanks all, talk soon.
